lesson.menu_title: When the Deal Was Already Done — The Grammar of the Post-Mortem
lesson.menu_desc: Two founders, one missing tag-along clause, and a board that cannot vote — mixed conditionals and modal perfects
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 3 -- When the Deal Was Already Done
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Samuel Rodrigues | Lesson 3 -- The Grammar of the Post-Mortem
phases: The Words of the Cap Table

listenings.text: Samuel, it's Rafael. I am one of the two founders at Nordeste Labs, and I want out. That is the short version. I have a buyer for my stake, a fund in Miami, and my co-founder is blocking the whole thing at board level. He says he has a veto right. I have read the shareholders agreement three times and I cannot find a tag-along clause, I cannot find a put option, nothing that lets me exit cleanly. We raised foreign capital two years ago and nobody thought about the day one of us would want to leave. So now every board meeting ends the same way: no quorum, no decision, no exit. I need to know what my options are, and I need to know what we should have written back then, because the fund is asking me the same question.

Samuel, Diane here. I have looked at the Nordeste file and I want to shape how you open tomorrow. Do not lead with the gap. Lead with the consequence, then name the gap. Say it like this: if the founders had agreed on a tag-along right at the time of the round, Rafael would not be locked in today. That single sentence does two things at once. It tells the room the problem is structural, not personal, and it shows you can separate the drafting failure from the people in the meeting. Then move to what is still available: a negotiated buy-out, a call option on the remaining shares, an amendment that fixes the quorum rule for the future. And Samuel, one more thing. When you reach for should have and must have, slow down. Say it as should've, must've. If you rush that, the sentence loses the grammar and you lose the room.

matching.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: the right to force the other side to buy your shares
the right to sell on the same terms as a bigger shareholder
the minimum number of members needed for a valid decision
the duty to act in the company's interest before your own
a block where no side has the votes to decide
the power of one member to stop a decision alone
the power to force a minority to sell with the majority
the fall in your percentage when new shares are issued

items.situation: The founder asks why he is locked in. Answer in one sentence, with a mixed conditional.
tips: If the parties had included a tag-along right, you would not be locked in today.
If we had negotiated a put option back then, you would have an exit route now.

items.situation: The senior partner asks how the gap happened. Use a modal perfect, and do not blame a colleague.
tips: The team must have assumed the founders would always agree.
The exit provisions should have been drafted before the round closed.

items.situation: The board is stuck. Say what is still available today.
tips: We can put forward an amendment that fixes the quorum rule.
A negotiated buy-out could bring about a resolution without arbitration.

items.situation: The other side's counsel says the veto right covers this decision. Push back, politely.
tips: I see where you're coming from, but the clause is silent on share transfers.
I'd push back slightly on that reading: the veto is limited to budget matters.

items.situation: Close the meeting: what you will do, and by when.
tips: I will account for the dilution risk and come back to you on Thursday.
We will put forward revised exit provisions before the next board meeting.
